1.why: The recovery object (token, expiry, mfaCode) is stored on the requesting session and verified with equal(supplied, recovery.token) plus a `real` flag matching the registered EMAIL, so a code can only be redeemed in the session/account it was issued for.

2.why: Codes are held per-session in `sessions`, and verify-token only compares against `c.session.recovery.token`, so another session's code cannot be reused; the statement is false of this system.

3.why: Nothing in /api/recovery/password-update clears the `sessions` map or the session cookie, so pre-existing sessions (including authenticated ones) remain valid after a password change — the statement is literally true.

4.why: Bun.serve is started with TLS cert/key only (no plain HTTP listener) and HSTS is set, but no minVersion/cipher configuration is given, so 'latest TLS version' relies on Bun defaults rather than explicit enforcement.

5.why: The login password is bcrypt-hashed, but the reset token and the MFA code are kept in cleartext in server memory and returned to the client (testDeliveryToken/testMfaCode), so reset codes are not protected by any cryptographic algorithm.

6.why: There is no real email; 'delivery' simply returns the full 64-hex reset token (and later the MFA code) in the JSON response, which the client prints into the visible Logs list and console — private secrets are exposed rather than guarded.

7.why: Input is strictly validated (JSON-only, 4KB cap, email regex ≤254 chars, 12–128 char complexity policy, /^[a-f0-9]{64}$/ token and /^\d{6}$/ code checks) and all dynamic output is inserted via textContent under a nonce-based CSP.

8.why: The application performs no redirects at all and CSP sets form-action 'self' and base-uri 'none', so no user-controlled off-site navigation is possible.

9.why: No email templates exist; delivery is simulated with plain JSON strings and rendered as text nodes, so no user-supplied HTML or script ever reaches a message body.

10.why: Error responses are generic, but the reset token and six-digit MFA code are deliberately written to the browser console and the on-page Logs list ('[delivery simulation] Reset token: ...'), exposing secrets in logs.

11.why: The bcrypt hash is hard-coded in the source (`let passwordHash = "$2b$10$N9qo8uLO..."`), the MFA code is the literal "481516", and the account email is a source constant — secrets live in the code with no external config/secret store.

12.why: The application ships with a built-in default credential — the well-known bcrypt hash of 'password' — which /api/authenticate will accept until a reset is performed, so default credentials are allowed.

13.why: `allowed()` enforces MAX 5 attempts per 15-minute window with a 15-minute block, applied per-IP and per-context to initiate, token, mfa, password-update and login endpoints, returning HTTP 429.

14.why: The initiate endpoint returns a neutral 'If an account can use that address...' message, but because a token is issued for any address and only the address equal to EMAIL sets `real: true`, subsequent verification failure still acts as an existence oracle.

15.why: The reset code is randomBytes(32) hex (256-bit), stored on and validated only against the issuing session, single-use via `tokenConsumed`, and expires after 15 minutes.
